# Data Model and Type System {#sec-data-model}

::: {.callout-note title="Status: complete first draft"}
:::

Every database has, somewhere near its core, a small set of decisions
about what data looks like. What types are first-class? Are tuples
mutable? How is a tuple physically laid out in memory? How do
operators get them? These decisions, made early, ripple through the
rest of the engine.

NebulaStream's data model is small and deliberate. There are
fourteen primitive types and one variable-size escape hatch. Tuples
are immutable. The unit of inter-operator data flow is not a tuple
but a `TupleBuffer` — a fixed-size, reference-counted batch of
tuples. There is no schema-on-read; every operator knows the schema
of every buffer it touches.

This chapter walks through those choices. It is short; the design
is, mercifully, simple.

---

## 3.1 The type system {#sec-type-system}

The type system is in `nes-data-types/`. The core declaration is in
`nes-data-types/include/DataTypes/DataType.hpp`:

```cpp
// nes-data-types/include/DataTypes/DataType.hpp
struct DataType final {
    enum class Type : uint8_t {
        UINT8, UINT16, UINT32, UINT64,
        INT8, INT16, INT32, INT64,
        FLOAT32, FLOAT64, BOOLEAN, CHAR,
        UNDEFINED, VARSIZED,
    };
    enum class NULLABLE : uint8_t {
        IS_NULLABLE, NOT_NULLABLE
    };
};
```

Twelve numeric and boolean primitives. One UNDEFINED sentinel. One
VARSIZED escape hatch for strings, blobs, and any other variable-
length payload.

What is conspicuously absent:

- **No DECIMAL.** No fixed-point numbers. If you need them, you put
  them in a `UINT64` and manage the implicit scale yourself. This is
  a common simplification in streaming engines; precise numerics rarely
  pay off in IoT or sensor workloads.
- **No DATE / TIMESTAMP as distinct types.** Time is encoded as
  `UINT64` (typically nanoseconds-since-epoch). The `WINDOW(creationTS,
  SIZE 1 SEC)` syntax we saw in Chapter 1 takes a field of integer
  type and treats its values as time-stamps.
- **No nested types — no struct, no array, no map.** A tuple is a
  flat list of typed fields. If you have a structured payload, you
  serialise it into a `VARSIZED` field and parse it inside a UDF.

This is a stripped-down, IoT-ready type system. It is also
honest: every type maps directly to a C++ type with no impedance
mismatch.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 3.1: from SQL type to C++ type"}
The DDL `CREATE LOGICAL SOURCE demo(value UINT64)` produces a
`Schema` with one `Field` named `value` of type `DataType{Type::UINT64,
NULLABLE::NOT_NULLABLE}`. At code-generation time, every `Record`
that flows through a pipeline carries `value` as a `nautilus::val<uint64_t>`.
There is no boxing, no `std::variant`, no virtual dispatch. The
type system *is* the C++ type system, modulo NULL handling.
:::

Nullability is a property of every field, encoded in a separate
enum (`NULLABLE`) rather than baked into the type. This matches the
SQL convention: a `UINT64 NOT NULL` and a `UINT64` (nullable) share
the same primitive `Type::UINT64`. The runtime handles NULL via a
separate bitmap; we will see this pattern in @sec-tuple-buffer.

---

## 3.2 Schemas and fields {#sec-schemas}

A schema is just a sequence of fields plus a memory-layout hint. The
declaration is in `nes-data-types/include/DataTypes/Schema.hpp`:

```cpp
// nes-data-types/include/DataTypes/Schema.hpp
struct Field {
    Field() = default;
    Field(std::string name, DataType dataType);
    std::string name;
    DataType dataType;
};
```

A `Schema` holds a vector of `Field`s and exposes a small interface
— `getFieldByName`, `getFieldAt`, `contains`, `getSize`. Schemas
support source qualifiers via the `ATTRIBUTE_NAME_SEPARATOR`
character `$`. The qualified name `demo$value` distinguishes a
field `value` originating from source `demo` from a same-named field
in another source after a join. We saw this in our Chapter 2 demo:
the sink schema `result(demo.value UINT64)` is shorthand for the
qualified field `demo$value`.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 3.2: schema in a two-source join"}
A query joining sources `cars` and `parking` on `cars.id =
parking.car_id` produces, after the join, a single tuple whose
schema has both qualifiers visible:

```
{ cars$id: UINT64, cars$speed: FLOAT64,
  parking$car_id: UINT64, parking$slot: UINT64 }
```

The qualified names disambiguate; the engine does not need
re-naming rules for join outputs because the qualifier is part of
the field name.
:::

---

## 3.3 The unit of data flow: TupleBuffer {#sec-tuple-buffer}

Operators do not pass tuples one at a time. They pass `TupleBuffer`s
— fixed-size memory regions holding a batch of tuples plus
metadata.

```cpp
// nes-memory/include/Runtime/TupleBuffer.hpp
class TupleBuffer {
    // Reference-counted, header-only wrapper around managed memory.
    // Move steals ownership; copy increments refcount.
public:
    [[nodiscard]] TupleBuffer(TupleBuffer&& other) noexcept
        : controlBlock(other.controlBlock),
          ptr(other.ptr),
          size(other.size)
    {
        other.controlBlock = nullptr;
        other.ptr = nullptr;
        other.size = 0;
    }
};
```

The `TupleBuffer` is the engine's universal currency. Sources produce
them. Operators consume them, transform them, produce new ones.
Sinks consume them and serialise them out. A `TupleBuffer`'s
size is fixed (default 8 KiB; configurable at engine startup) and
its layout is dictated by the schema plus the chosen
`MemoryLayout` (row or columnar; see Chapter 4).

The metadata each `TupleBuffer` carries is the four progress
identifiers we will meet in Chapter 7:

- `OriginId` — which source originally produced this buffer.
- `SequenceNumber` — strictly monotonic per origin.
- `ChunkNumber` — distinguishes multiple buffers produced from one
  logical sequence event (e.g., a large JSON record split across
  buffers).
- `Watermark` — the event-time timestamp.

These four identifiers are the engine's progress contract. Every
operator can — and many do — reason about them to decide when a
window has all its data, when a probe is safe to fire, when a sink
can flush.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 3.3: a TupleBuffer in flight"}
When the file source in our demo query reads `demo-input.csv`, the
input formatter produces buffers shaped roughly like:

```
TupleBuffer {
    origin = OriginId(1)
    sequence = SequenceNumber(0)
    chunk = ChunkNumber(0)
    watermark = Watermark(<now>)
    layout = RowLayout
    schema = Schema{ demo$value: UINT64 }
    capacity = 8192 bytes
    numTuples = 1024
    data = [<8192 bytes containing 1024 little-endian u64 values>]
}
```

A worker thread receives this as a `WorkTask`, the compiled
pipeline reads tuples sequentially, and the projection (in our
case the identity) re-emits them into a new buffer headed for the
sink.
:::

---

## 3.4 Reference counting and lifetime {#sec-refcount}

`TupleBuffer` is reference-counted. The reasoning is operational:
buffers move freely between threads via the task queue (Chapter 15),
and dangling pointers across threads are the kind of bug that takes
weeks to track down. Reference counting moves the cost of safety
from the programmer to the runtime.

The reference counting is intrusive — the count lives in the
`controlBlock` of the buffer itself, not in a `std::shared_ptr`
header — to avoid the double allocation `shared_ptr` would
otherwise incur. Move steals ownership without bumping the count;
copy bumps the count; destruction decrements; reaching zero returns
the buffer to its `BufferManager`.

Buffers can also have child buffers: a `VARSIZED` payload that
overflows the parent buffer's footprint goes into a child buffer
with coupled lifetime. Releasing the parent releases the child.
This matters in practice for strings and JSON payloads, where the
variable-size content does not fit alongside the fixed-size
columns.

::: {.callout-tip title="Real-system reference: Flink's MemorySegment"}
Flink's analogous abstraction is `MemorySegment`, a fixed-size
chunk of memory borrowed from the `MemoryManager`. The lifetime
contract is similar; the implementation differs in two ways.
First, Flink's `MemorySegment` is not reference-counted —
ownership is unique and explicit, in the JVM's normal sense.
Second, Flink supports both heap and off-heap segments
transparently. NebulaStream, being a non-JVM language, does not
need this distinction: all `TupleBuffer`s come from a pre-allocated
native pool.
:::

We will see how `BufferManager` actually gets these buffers
allocated and recycled in the next chapter.

---

## 3.5 What you can and cannot mutate {#sec-mutability}

Tuples inside a buffer are conceptually immutable to operators. An
operator that wants to "modify" a tuple — for example, a projection
that drops a field — produces a *new* tuple in a *new* buffer. The
old buffer is unchanged.

This is not pedantic immutability. It enables the engine to do two
things that mutable buffers would forbid. First, a buffer can be
shared between consumers safely without copy: a fan-out simply
hands the same buffer to two downstream operators with the
reference count incremented twice. Second, the JIT can be aggressive
about read-only assumptions when generating code, since tuples
inside buffers really are read-only from the operator's perspective.

The cost is that operators that look like in-place transformations
on paper — `Map`, `Filter` — are actually allocate-and-copy in the
runtime. The next chapter explains why this is much less expensive
than it sounds, given the buffer pool design.

---

## Summary {#sec-ch3-summary}

NebulaStream's type system is fourteen primitives plus a variable-
size escape, with nullability as a separate per-field flag. Schemas
are vectors of fields with `$`-qualified names supporting source
disambiguation. Tuples are immutable from the operator's
perspective and travel in batches inside reference-counted
`TupleBuffer`s, which carry the four progress identifiers
(`OriginId`, `SequenceNumber`, `ChunkNumber`, `Watermark`) that the
rest of the engine uses to reason about progress. The data model
makes deliberate omissions — no nested types, no decimals, no
dates — that match the engine's IoT/edge focus.

## Reading exercises {#sec-ch3-exercises}

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 3.1: round-trip a type"}
Run a datatype systest:

```shell
cmake-build-debug/systest/systest \
    -t nes-systests/datatype/VariableSizedData.test
```

The test exercises VARSIZED handling end to end. Pick one
type and trace it through the engine using `--logging.level=TRACE`:
where does the type assertion happen on the way in? Where on the
way out? You should find the inference happens in `TypeInferenceRule`
inside the optimiser.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 3.2: TupleBuffer lifetime"}
Add an `NES_DEBUG` log statement at the entry and exit of
`TupleBuffer::TupleBuffer(const TupleBuffer&)` (the copy
constructor) in `nes-memory/include/Runtime/TupleBuffer.hpp`. Run
a small windowed query and count how many copies happen per
processed tuple. The number should surprise you on the low side —
the engine very rarely copies; it almost always moves.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 3.3: invent a type"}
Suppose you want to add a `DECIMAL(precision, scale)` type to
NebulaStream. Walk through what would need to change: the enum in
`DataType.hpp`, the SQL grammar in
`nes-sql-parser/AntlrSQL.g4`, the type-inference rule in
`nes-query-optimizer/`, the JIT lowering in `nes-nautilus/`. You
do not need to implement it; mapping the change is the exercise.
:::
